posts.author: Hans
posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
I have found that 2-component epoxy attacks the gelatin and that cyanoacryalate (super glue) does not harden well on the super dry emulsion. As I was not prepared to cut away the DCG from the sides of the developed plate and sandwich in glass that way, I tried "transparent molding resin" from MakeMe. I think it is a polyester resin because the activator contains methyl keton peroxide.

It is simple to mix and the mixture can be poured on the hologram after any tiny bubbles have disappeared. Then a cover plate can be pushed onto the hologram and after about 3 hours the resin has hardened, leaving a perfectly clear hologram. 

(I suspect this is the same stuff that is used for polyester top-coating garage floors and walls to make them more moisture and dust resistant.)

posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
Hans, you are going to find out that if you do not scrape away the emulsion from the edge of the glass your hologram will start to disappear over time from the outside in. Let me explain why.

If you looked at a cross section of the sealed hologram the way you explain it here is what you would see. First you will have glass, then emulsion, then the sealing agent then glass again. Having this edge of emulsion exposed to the air will be the downfall of the hologram. As gelatin is very hydroscopic, it will eventually absorb moisture from the air at this edge and pass the moisture eventually destroying the hologram. 

I know of at least one person that used to seal their hologram in a similar manner and then shape the final hologram with a grinder. This left the emulsion edge exposed as I just described. Every one of the holograms I bought from this person have start to disappear from the edge in after only a year or so.

So my suggestion is to still clear emulsion from the edge of the hologram then seal it with the sealant you have found. UV epoxy works great but is outrageously expensive. If your resin does in fact work and is less expensive then it is a very exciting find. 

Do you know what the index of refraction is for this resin? Do you have a link I can research. If the index of refraction is close to that of glass and gelatin, then it would work great for HOE's and Masters.

posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** .............I did try UV glue. It worked fine, but the stuff costs 8 Euro for 2ml here. It's very viscous and that means that about 1ml is needed to seal one plate.

A DIY UV sealant

In keeping with the grand DIY philosophy of the Forum I thought I would put down some basic ingredients for making your own out of materials which are fundamentally cheap because of their big industrial use.

However before that a hypothesis that fits observations I have made. 

I believe that the reason DCG has been so notoriously difficult to seal up 

and prevent moisture getting in is not necessarily due to any fault of hydrophobic glues being somehow rather more moisture pervious than expected. I believe the real trouble has been that sandwiched between 2 glass sheets the gelatin layer contracts with age and builds up a significant vacuum. This results eventually in outside air getting through microcracks inspite of diligently thick glue having been applied around the edges of the sandwich.. This contraction effect might be just to do with the basic properties of the gelatin under prolonged lighting but it could well be more to do with the final stubborn traces of water /alcohol still hanging about and alcohol vapour can very gradually (we can be talking “years” here) make its way through the edge sealant increasing the vacuum effect. Anyway whatever the cause an obvious way to minimise it is to put the newly processed DCG in a really dry warmer I am not sure what temperature is best but 60-70C for as long 24 hours seems to work or alternatively I have left them in a really effective desiccator for a week. Then without giving the ultra dry DCG a chance to re-absorb ambient humidity a dry glass cover plate with dry sealant 

can be put on. This topic has been discussed on the forum before and some of you guys have had vastly more experience than me at sealing. 

To make a UV curable sealant,you need a monomer, crosslinker, and free radical generator for UV.

Monomer :

 Methyl methacrylate or better (more hydrophobic) is butyl methacrylate (NB. Not tert-butyl methacrylate)

Crosslinker: 

 Ethylene dimethacrylate (alternative silly name by Sigma Aldrich is ethylene glycol dimethacrylate).

UV sensitizer (free radical generator in UV.):

DMPA or dimethoxyphenyl acetophenone.

One can use about 1 part DMPA to 100 parts monomer to 5-10 parts crosslinker.

It gets harder the more crosslinker you add of course. (~80-100% crosslinker just cracks up). 

But the mix has initially a rather low viscosity , lower than the commercial stuff.

It is a good idea to store mixture over silica gel in a fridge in the dark.

Jeff

posts.topic_title: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md: All adhesives will no doubt absorb water over time, but this in itself should not pose any problem for sealing DCG. It's not the adhesive itself that really counts, but rather the quality of adhesion to glass. Of course, a water-resistant adhesive such as epoxy should be used (I plan to use another type of adhesive, but epoxy should probably do about as well from the standpoint of water-resistance through the bulk of the adhesive). But epoxy is not especially good at long-term adherence to glass, when the glass has not received any special treatment. It's deceptive, because the bond seems good at first, but over time (months or years) if often pulls away from the glass surface. Blyth has speculated that cracks may be formed (exactly where, he didn't say) due pressure-stresses caused by a vacuum being generated when DCG holograms are sealed using epoxy. However, epoxy-on-glass bonds will also fail without any such pressure. I believe the failure is simply caused due to the long-term effect of water vapor at the interface. This effect has been researched and documented in great detail, see for example *Moisture-assisted crack growth at epoxy-glass interfaces*, Journal of Materials Science **33** (1998) pages 4581-4588.

I would be concerned about the quality of the adhesive itself though. Maybe I am a bit overly sensitive about that. As you know, some time ago I tried to do the “opposite” of DCG - sealing wet recorded/replayed silver halide holograms. Back then I was unable finding an adhesive (anything from epoxies to cyanacrylates, UV curing acrylic adhesives, oils, natural resins etc.) that resisted the vapor pressure built up within the glass-film-glass sandwich for more than a few days. By the way, the best solution finally consisted of using glycerol/water mixtures, which at least lasted for several months. 

Nowadays, I think the thing could be done in a much simpler way by sealing the hologram within a high barrier plastic.

I wonder if DCG sealing would be more efficient on such grounds.

And one other thing comes to my mind in that context: the manufacturing process of safety glass for automobile windshields. I understand it's a hot laminating process based on PVB (polyvinyl butyral) resin.

I've never heard about issues of “humidity” regarding those safety glasses.

posts.topic_title: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
Thanks, Colin, for your comments, I appreciate it.

> **Martin:** Joe wrote:All adhesives will no doubt absorb water over time, but this in itself should not pose any problem for sealing DCG. It's not the adhesive itself that really counts, but rather the quality of adhesion to glass.I would be concerned about the quality of the adhesive itself though.

I definitely agree. Maybe I should have made that clearer, but I wanted to stress the importance of the adhesive-to-glass bond. I also agree about the use of a silane, under certain circumstances. Actually, I feel that a good-quality epoxy, applied carefully to silane-prepared glass, should be quite adequate for DCG holograms. The paper I mentioned offered that solution to the problem, and their tests indicated that the epoxy to silane-prepared glass was so strong, that, under stress, failure often occurred in the bulk of the glass, rather than at the glass-to-epoxy interface!

As to how well silane-prepared glass does with other adhesives remains something of an open question for me. But the results have been well-documented in the case of epoxy.

As you mentioned, there are a lot of tantalizing things in industry regarding the permanent adhesion of glass to glass, or glass to other surfaces. One other thing I've noted is two-pane window glass (insulated windows) with an inert gas inside (for energy efficiency). I have two of these windows in my lab, which I had installed in 1992. The gap between the panes must be under considerable vacuum (to contain the inert gas) since the panes are obviously slightly curved. Maybe other people have noticed these types of windows, which do not produce "flat" reflections when they are looked at. Anyway, those must be very high-reliability bonds to be used in such an extreme environment, exposed to the outside in all types of weather. About a month ago, one of those seals failed, and one of the panes shattered (on the inside of the lab). The sudden stress of coming "up to air" must have been too much for it, since it was bent inward for all those years. I did get a chance to examine the adhesive, though. It was an extremely sticky black substance. (Who knows what it was.)

Joe you state, "Actually, I feel that a good-quality epoxy, applied carefully to silane-prepared glass, should be quite adequate for DCG holograms."

I have to question this. I have been doing DCG for about 6 years now and I have my first DCG's that have been hanging on the wall all this time. posts.topic_title: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
John, all I can say is that many years of experience with epoxy has made me nervous about it. It all depends on your needs. Both epoxy and UV adhesive, carefully applied without the use of silane, may hold indefinitely, if they are kept under normal indoor conditions.

The problem arises when the humidity, for some reason, goes up to about 80% or more, and stays there for a prolonged period (days or weeks or months). If silane is not used on the glass beforehand, I would expect failure in that case. It doesn't take "complete delamination" in the sense that the glass comes completely off. It just takes a harline crack, literally the width of a hair or smaller, to introduce mositure. Many years of experience with epoxy on glass has shown me that failure is highly irregular in nature, some areas adhering stongly to the glass with no sign of delamination, while other areas on the same piece showing tiny areas of delamination, visible by the different way light is transmitted through it.

If losing a hologram isn't a catastrophe for you, and you don't let the holograms stay above 80% humidity for days or weeks, then they should probably last a long time, perhaps even indefinitely in some cases, without silane preparation. But if you take a close look at glass conservation literature involving the use epoxy, the importance of the silane becomes apparent. Perhaps you are familar with the epoxy called Hxtal NYL-1. This is probably the most prestigious epoxy used in glass conservation (from the standpoint of permanence), and an important part of the Hxtal system is the use of a silane preparation for the glass. They wouldn't go though this hassle if it wasn't important. But actually it's not a hassle, just an extra step in the process. If we really care about the permanence of our DCG holograms, one extra step shouldn't be a big deal.

For reference, see:

*Review of CCI research on epoxy resin adhesives for glass conseravtion*, by Jane L. Down

*Crack propagation in polymer adhesive/glass sandwich specimens*, Journal of Adhesion (1995) Vol. 49, pages 97-112

*Subcritical crack growth along epoxy/glass int*erfaces, J. Mater. Res., Vol. 7, No. 9, pages 2621-29 (1992)

A book called *Conservation of Glass* by Newman/Davidson (1989)

Also, there is a voluminous literature on silane coupling agents.

Note also the silane for the Hxtal system at:

[http://www.hisglassworks.com/cart/cart. ... etail&p=96](http://www.hisglassworks.com/cart/cart.php?m=product_detail&p=96)

Still no failures at all. Some I have sealed this way have been in the lab in which I only keep the heat on to 55F when I don't use it and I am sure the humidity has been as high as 78% at 80F in the summer.So the above I believe is more then adequate.

This is my std procedure for sealing MBDCG holograms, I have 3 yrs old holos and the are still beatiful):

1- Clean a clear glass plate same size (or bigger) of the holo plate

2- with a sharp knife, remove about 3-5mm of gelatine from edges of the holo plate

3- heat the glass plate (emulsion side) with hair dryer. This step must be done very carefully (slowly) to avoid humidity condensation into the emulsion (hologram rapidally desappears)

4- put both plates in a heated (~70C) oven for 10 minutes

5- remove plates form the oven and seal with epoxy glue. This operation must be done with hot plates.

6- put the sandwich into the oven (~50C) for 30 minutes.

I used the following glues: Araldite, Pattex, Saratoga with the same results

posts.topic_title: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
I would like to make a few last comments on this subject. The whole point is DCG hologram longevity, in particular what is meant by "longevity."

If a DCG hologram is kept in a normal, indoor, year-round living area, then the techniques described by John and Cristiano may do very well for many years, and, perhaps (as I said above), indefinitely. So in other words, if you keep the hologram with you, (essentially "living with it") in your house or apartment, then that is one set of circumstances. In colder enviroments (in which many of us live), indoor conditions can get very dry for long periods, due to central heating. (This is no problem, of course.) Things can get very damp too, but this is usually for brief periods, at least where I am. As I mentioned before, problems occur when the dampness lasts for days, weeks, or months. So under normal indoor conditions, this doesn't really happen, at least where I live. So, again, there is no real problem for the types of sealing techniques described by John and Cristiano.

However, there is something else which needs to be considered, if you intend to place your hologram into the hands of another person, or intend to sell one. Namely, conditions outside the "normal." Would you like to sell your hologram for a decent price and have to say "Oh, by the way, the hologram can't be allowed to stay above 80% RH for a month, or it will start to vanish?

Living conditions and storage conditions can be two utterly different things. In an unheated storage building, the humidity can easily go above 80% and stay there for a long time. I have a nice hologram by August Muth which was stored in such a building, and the edge started to delaminate irregularly, causing the edge to vanish. Luckily, I caught this in time, and brought it inside the house, and it didn't seem to deteriorate any further. 

Or, think about storage in a damp basement, or in any environment where the humidity is not controlled. Holograms do no always hang on the wall. People may get tired of them, and put them into storage.

Or, think about other climates where it is very damp.

Do you guys think I like these complications? Do you think I enjoy worrying about this stuff? Not at all. It's just that I'm "serious" about sealing DCG holograms, for good reasons.

posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
After reflection, I'm not sure whether varying the amount of epoxy hardener (within reasonable bounds) actually affects the final hardness or if it just affects the time it takes to finally cure rock-hard. Some research is needed - maybe there are epoxy formulations that work better with glass than the common 2-part mixes.

Also - something that would be very useful for comparing DCG sealing techniques is an easily reproduced accelerated life test method. Say, for example, placing the fully cured sample in a freezer for a minute, removing to room temperature and allowing condensation, then a 100 degree oven for a minute and repeating these steps some large number (20-50?) times. If this at least weeded out bad sealing methods it would be helpful.

posts.content_md:
> **Tom B.:** After reflection, I'm not sure whether varying the amount of epoxy hardener (within reasonable bounds) actually affects the final hardness or if it just affects the time it takes to finally cure rock-hard. Some research is needed - maybe there are epoxy formulations that work better with glass than the common 2-part mixes.

I know that varying the mix affects the final hardness of JB-weld. Using more steel results in a slightly rubbery epoxy. I have some that's stayed that way for two years.

It's possible that other epoxies behave differently but I'd guess not as long as they were all mixed thoroughly.

posts.topic_title: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Good way to seal a DCG hologram
posts.content_md:
> **Tom B.:** I wonder too if modifying the epoxy resin/hardener proportions (using less hardener so the cured epoxy was not so rigid) would provide a more tenacious, less easily cracked bond.

I don't know the answer to that, but Hxtal is specially formulated for glass, and it uses 3 parts resin to 1 part hardener. So you may have a point. Also, mixed Hxtal has a thinner consistency than the hardware-store type of epoxy. This, combined with the slow curing time, may be important to thoroughly "wet" the glass. Just guessing here.

Surprisingly, that black substance holding my window-panes under vacuum was not hard, and it really stretched out when I was pulling fragments of glass out of the window frame. It was about the consistency of chewing gum (already chewed) that has been allowed to dry out for several days. But it was incredibly, incredibly sticky. (Other industrial applications for high-quality epoxy for bonding glass include vacuum-related uses. As I recall, the stuff was called Torr Seal.)

But I've heard that the brewster windows on the SP-125, supposedly attached with some kind of epoxy, do eventually fail. This is something I haven't experienced myself, though, and I do know that the 125's can last for a very long time. So, if they are really glued with epoxy, I would like to know what kind of epoxy it was, and if they used any special preparation techniques for the glass.

> **Joe:** ... what is meant by "longevity."

In the context of image permanence, every then and there I wonder:

why is it such clearcut evidence that glass lasts “forever” (of course - unless it gets broken), whereas plastic materials are supposed to reach a few years at best?

For example, CD materials (I guess mostly polycarbonate) have been submitted to extensive artificial aging tests. They're said to easily reach 50 or even more than 150 years.

posts.content_md:
> **Martin:** In the context of image permanence....I wonder: why is it such clearcut evidence that glass lasts “forever”....

That's perhaps the greatest reason of all for getting "serious" about sealing DCG holograms. People have the perception that they're dealing with a "glass" item, when in fact its vulnerability lies in its non-glass component.
